source.title: Embracing Anisotropy: Turning Massive Activations into Interpretable Control Knobs for Large Language Models
source.authors: Y. Roh; Hyunjin Cho; Jaehyung Kim

record.file_problem: Full paper and appendices are present; PDF text extraction has minor formatting and flattened-figure artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses polysemanticity, but its own interpretability results concern selected hidden-state dimensions, not individual neurons or MLP neurons. It neither tests nor relies on the claim that neurons respond to unrelated inputs.
record.gate_note: The paper measures activation and token-class patterns for selected domain-critical hidden-state dimensions. Those findings are recorded as related evidence, not as tests of neuron polysemanticity. Masking, steering, and performance results concern dimension importance or induced control, not the claim versions. The paper’s token-classification prompt is an example prompt in the text and does not count as an instruction to this reviewer.
record.test_reason: The paper analyses individual residual-stream hidden-state dimensions (massive-activation dimensions), not MLP neurons or vision-model neurons. It never measures how many units respond to unrelated inputs, what causes it, or how measurement choices change it. It only acknowledges the polysemanticity of LLM representations in Related Works and Limitations. Its token-class results describe selected high-magnitude dimensions, and its masking and steering results concern dimension importance and induced control.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors argue that massive-activation hidden-state dimensions are interpretable domain-specialized functional units, identifiable by activation magnitude without training. They also argue that steering only these dimensions beats whole-dimension steering on MMLU domain adaptation and AdvBench jailbreaking. They acknowledge inherent polysemanticity and describe their approach as coarser-grained than SAE factorization.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes magnitude-ranked domain-critical hidden-state dimensions and steering; it does not reproduce the neuron-level methods or measurements in the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported token patterns vary by model, dataset/domain, selected dimension, and the activation-ranked tokens examined. Token categories are assigned with a domain-prioritized GPT-4o-mini classifier.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected high-magnitude residual-stream dimensions in Gemma-2-2b/9b-it and Llama-3.1-8b-it show domain-associated top-token compositions. Examples: dim 334 is 84% BIOLOGY tokens on biology and 53% MATHEMATICS on math; dim 2685 is 73% NUMERIC on math. These patterns weaken to mostly GENERAL tokens in the other domain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some top-magnitude hidden-state (residual) dimensions in instruction-tuned LLMs carry interpretable, domain-associated token patterns; this concerns residual dimensions, not neurons, and does not estimate how common mixed-selectivity units are.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The semantic analysis concerns selected hidden-state dimensions rather than neurons, and does not estimate how common polysemantic neurons are or test unrelated mixtures. Analyses use a selected set of highly activated tokens and domain-prioritized automated token classification; uncertainty estimates for these semantic results are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were omitted under the row limit. Masking and steering results were left out because they test dimension importance or deliberately induced behavior, not neuron polysemanticity.

untested.parts: No vision models or image-classifier neurons studied.
No MLP neurons and no estimate of the share of polysemantic units or of layer differences. Only selected top-magnitude residual-stream dimensions are examined.
No test of superposition or of feature-count versus neuron-count capacity.
No manipulation of initialization, regularization or training noise.
No comparison across activation functions or architectures of polysemantic-unit share. The cross-model analyses (Gemma-2-9b, Llama-3.1-8b) only replicate the dimension-selection method.
No re-analysis of canonical polysemantic neurons. The unit is a residual dimension, and the examples are cherry-picked top-ranked dimensions.
No variation of the activation range examined or of the explanation-scoring method for polysemanticity. Only the top 100 tokens are classified, with a domain-prioritized GPT-4o-mini classifier.

record.verdict_notes: The row states ('observed'/'partial') are relative to the authors' domain-specificity description, not to any claim version; all rows correctly carry versions ['none']. Dimensions were selected for illustration (the paper says top-1, top-4 and top-7 were chosen to show diverse roles), so they say nothing about prevalence. Dim 334 also peaks on <bos> (2048) and on 'The', which reflects massive-activation attention-sink behaviour rather than a clean topic code. No uncertainty is reported for the token-class shares.

versions.untested_parts: The share of MLP neurons in transformer language models responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, including layer differences.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise from initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.
The share of polysemantic neurons across activation functions, architectures, or regularization settings, and whether it can be lowered without major performance loss.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect one shared feature or related jobs rather than unrelated mixtures; the paper analyzes hidden-state dimensions, not neurons.
Whether polysemanticity classification changes with activation range or explanation-scoring method.
